title: Chapter 46 — Surmises
paragraphs: Though, consumed by the hot fire of his purpose, Ahab in all his thoughts and actions always had in view the ultimate capture of Moby Dick; though he seemed ready to sacrifice all mortal interests to that one passion; it may nevertheless have been that he was by nature and long habit far too wedded to a fiery whaleman's ways to give up altogether pursuing the ordinary business of the voyage alongside it. Or at least, if this was not so, there was no lack of other motives with much more influence on him. It would perhaps be too fine a point, even allowing for his monomania, to hint that his vindictiveness toward the White Whale might possibly have extended in some degree to all sperm whales, and that the more monsters he killed, the more he multiplied the chances that each whale he met afterward would prove to be the hated one he hunted. But if such a hypothesis is indeed open to objection, there were still further considerations which, though not so strictly in keeping with the wildness of his ruling passion, were by no means incapable of swaying him.

To accomplish his object Ahab had to use tools; and of all tools used in the shadow of the moon, men are the most apt to get out of order. He knew, for example, that however magnetic his ascendancy over Starbuck was in some respects, that ascendancy did not cover the whole spiritual man, any more than mere bodily superiority implies intellectual mastery; for to the purely spiritual, the intellectual stands only in a sort of bodily relation. Starbuck's body and Starbuck's coerced will were Ahab's, so long as Ahab kept his magnet at Starbuck's brain; still, he knew that for all this the chief mate in his soul abhorred his captain's quest, and if he could, would joyfully cut himself loose from it, or even thwart it. It might be a long time before the White Whale was seen. During that long interval Starbuck would always be liable to fall into open relapses of rebellion against his captain's leadership, unless some ordinary, prudential, circumstantial influences were brought to bear on him. Not only that, but the subtle insanity of Ahab concerning Moby Dick was nowhere more significantly shown than in his superlative sense and shrewdness in foreseeing that, for the present, the hunt should somehow be stripped of the strange imaginative impiety that naturally clothed it; that the full terror of the voyage must be kept back in the dim background (for few men's courage can hold out against long brooding unrelieved by action); and that when they stood their long night watches, his officers and men must have some nearer things to think about than Moby Dick. For however eagerly and impetuously the savage crew had hailed the announcement of his quest, all sailors of every sort are more or less capricious and unreliable — they live in the changing outer weather, and they breathe in its fickleness — and when they are kept at the pursuit of some remote and blank object, however much it promises life and passion in the end, it is above all necessary that temporary interests and occupations should intervene and hold them healthily suspended for the final dash.

Nor did Ahab forget another thing. In times of strong emotion mankind scorns all base considerations; but such times are fleeting. The permanent, constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness. Granted that the White Whale fully stirs the hearts of this savage crew of mine, and, playing around their savageness, even breeds a certain generous knight-errantry in them — still, while they chase Moby Dick for the love of it, they must also have food for their more common, everyday appetites. For even the lofty, chivalric Crusaders of old were not content to cross two thousand miles of land to fight for their holy sepulchre without committing burglaries, picking pockets, and gaining other pious perks along the way. Had they been held strictly to their one final and romantic object, too many would have turned from that final and romantic object in disgust. I will not strip these men, thought Ahab, of all hope of cash — yes, cash. They may scorn cash now; but let some months go by with no prospect of it in view, and then this same dormant cash, suddenly mutinying in them, would soon cashier Ahab — dismiss him from his command.

There was yet another precautionary motive, more closely related to Ahab personally. Having revealed the prime but private purpose of the Pequod's voyage — impulsively, it is probable, and perhaps somewhat prematurely — Ahab was now fully aware that in doing so he had indirectly laid himself open to the unanswerable charge of usurpation; and with perfect impunity, both moral and legal, his crew, if they were so inclined and able to carry it out, could refuse all further obedience to him, and even take the command from him by force. Ahab must of course have been most anxious to protect himself from even the barest hint of a charge of usurpation, and from the possible consequences of such a suppressed feeling gaining ground. That protection could lie only in his own dominating brain and heart and hand, backed by a careful, closely calculating attention to every minute atmospheric influence to which his crew could possibly be subjected.

For all these reasons, and others perhaps too subtle to spell out here, Ahab plainly saw that he must still in good measure stay true to the natural, stated purpose of the Pequod's voyage — observe all customary practices, and not only that, but force himself to show all his well-known passionate interest in the general pursuit of his profession.

However that may be, his voice could now often be heard hailing the three mastheads, urging the men to keep a sharp lookout and to report even a porpoise. It did not take long for this vigilance to pay off.
